html:
The Windrush generation are the people from the Caribbean who settled in Britain between 1948 and 1971. They are named after the HMT Empire Windrush, a ship that landed hundreds of Caribbean migrants at Tilbury near London on 22 June 1948.

After the Second World War, Britain was short of workers to rebuild, and the new National Health Service, London Transport and factories recruited abroad. The British Nationality Act of 1948 made people of the colonies citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies, free to come and live in Britain. Many from Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados and elsewhere came, often expecting a welcome in what they had been taught was the mother country.

They met racism in housing and work, and riots in Notting Hill in 1958. They also built communities, churches and the Notting Hill Carnival, and changed British music, food and sport. Laws in 1962 and 1971 closed this open door.

In 2018 the Windrush scandal broke. Many who had come legally as children had never been given papers, and some were wrongly detained, denied care or deported. The government apologised and set up a compensation scheme.
